subject: Stream-start SLO checklist, demo agenda + pilot next steps
messages:
From: Jonas Weber <jonas@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Patel <samir@maplepay.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 14 Feb 2027 15:02:00 -0700
Subject: Stream-start SLO checklist, demo agenda + pilot next steps

Samir / Lucy —

Thanks again for the call earlier; appreciate the clear articulation of the payment confirmation use case and latency sensitivity. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned: 

Summary of requirements we heard:
- Primary SLO: time-to-first-token (stream start) <= 180 ms p95 for interactive receipts (peak region: us-east).
- Sustained throughput target: ~350 requests/sec during peak batch windows, with expected concurrency of 60-80 live sessions.
- Responses are streamed to the client via SSE or WebSocket (you prefer SSE for browser clients).
- Chunk cadence: smaller, more frequent chunks (ideally 100–200ms cadence) to enable progressive UI updates; average chunk size expected ~500–1,200 bytes.
- Fallback: when streaming is unavailable, clients should accept full response payloads with TTFT target relaxed to 300 ms.

Proposed immediate next steps:
1) Technical deep-dive (1 hr) with our runtime SEs — Ben and Lauren — to validate shapes and confirm a pilot config (concurrency, batching, cache settings). I propose Tue 16 Feb, 10:00–11:00 PT.
2) You send sample payloads (schema + 3 typical prompt sizes) and a short traffic profile (qps distribution by hour). We attached a sample payload template.
3) We'll produce a provisional SLO matrix and pilot plan (load window + success criteria). Expect that by EOD Wed.

Attachments: maplepay-sample-payloads.json (small sample schemas).

Questions for you ahead of the deep-dive:
- Can you confirm whether client connections will originate from browsers only, or also from server-side jobs (affects SSE vs WebSocket choice)?
- Any regulatory constraints that would require on-prem/private deployment for this workload?

Thanks — will follow up with calendar invite pending confirmation.

— Jonas
Jonas Weber
Enterprise AE, Redwood Inference
jonas@redwood.ai
+1 (415) 555-0198
From: Samir Patel <samir@maplepay.com>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas@redwood.ai>
Cc: Lucy Chen <lucy@maplepay.com>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 15 Feb 2027 09:28:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Stream-start SLO checklist, demo agenda + pilot next steps

Thanks Jonas — useful recap. A few clarifications from our side: 

- The 180 ms TTFT p95 target is correct for the customer-facing web checkout flows. Server-to-server reporting (back-office jobs) can tolerate higher TTFT (~400 ms).
- Clients: primarily browsers (SSE preferred). We have a handful of mobile apps that currently use WebSockets; those are lower priority for the initial pilot but we want to ensure the runtime can support both eventually.
- Peak windows: typically 16:00–18:00 ET with a ~20% spike, otherwise steady at ~120–150 qps. The 350 qps number I gave earlier was an overestimate — rechecked with infra. Peak concurrent sessions during the window are ~70.

We'll attach two sample payloads and a short qps-by-hour CSV before the deep-dive.

One ask: can you confirm whether the 100–200 ms chunk cadence is something Redwood can control at the runtime level (i.e., you can tune chunk flush frequency independent of model logits generation)?

— Samir
Samir Patel
Head of Platform, MaplePay
samir@maplepay.com
From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Patel <samir@maplepay.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 16 Feb 2027 11:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Stream-start SLO checklist, demo agenda + pilot next steps

Samir —

Short answers before the deep-dive: 

- Runtime control over chunk cadence: yes. Our serving runtime exposes flush cadence and chunk-size heuristics. We can prioritize low-latency flushes (100–200 ms) at the cost of slightly reduced batching efficiency. For the pilot we recommend enabling aggressive prefix/KV caching and a low-latency flush policy.

- TTFT vs model compute: TTFT is influenced by model cold-starts, tokenization costs, and network stack. For browser SSE flows, we typically deliver first chunk within 80–220 ms depending on model size and sequence length. Achieving consistent p95 <= 180 ms will be feasible if:
  * model is < 7B or is a quantized 7B variant for this workload,
  * request size (prompt + context) stays under ~1,500 tokens for the interactive path, and
  * we run with modest concurrency per GPU (we propose reserving dedicated capacity for the pilot to guarantee tail latencies).

- Throughput and concurrency: with a 4-GPU dedicated pool using continuous batching and the above settings we can sustain 350 qps with 70 concurrent sessions for the short pilot window. We'll produce a recommended capacity config in the pilot doc.

I'll bring an example SLO matrix and an ops playbook to the call (including monitoring hooks, trace keys, and rollout/fallback policies).

Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
ben@redwood.ai
From: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Patel <samir@maplepay.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 17 Feb 2027 09:13:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Stream-start SLO checklist, demo agenda + pilot next steps

Samir —

Thanks for the clarifications. Calendar invite sent for Tue 16 (we adjusted to your preferred slot); Ben and I will lead the technical portion.

Pre-read and what we'll bring:
- Proposed SLO matrix (attached: proposed-slo-matrix.xlsx) with targets per flow (interactive vs back-office) and observability signals to track.
- Chunk cadence examples and recommended runtime toggles (attached: chunk-cadence-examples.md).
- A lightweight load test plan and success criteria for the pilot (target: p95 TTFT <= 180 ms for interactive paths during the 30-minute peak window).

Action items for MaplePay before the meeting:
1) Share the sample payloads and qps-by-hour CSV (Samir to upload).
2) Confirm whether you want the pilot on Dedicated capacity vs Hosted with reserved burst — we recommend Dedicated for tail guarantees.
3) Provide an internal contact for networking/allowlist (if you want us to test from your staging VPC).

We’ll also include a short checklist to test progressive-render behavior in your front-end (edge timeouts, SSE reconnects).

Thanks — looking forward to the call.

— Lauren
Lauren Bishop
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
lauren@redwood.ai
